the end zone, the **end line**, acts like a safety that never misses. Zones, meanwhile, get
crowded and leaky; there is little room to drop into and receivers are always near a seam. So
defenses spend their deep defenders on the rush or on more man coverage. (The red zone gets its
own chapter: [Red Zone, Goal Line, and Short Yardage](../10-situational-football/10-03-red-zone-goal-line-and-short-yardage.qmd).)

**Talent.** Man coverage is only as good as the worst matchup in it, so teams with great
cornerbacks play more of it. In nflverse charting, the Patriots played man on a larger share of
dropbacks than any other defense in 2018 and 2019 (about 61% and 68%), the seasons around Stephon
Gilmore's Defensive Player of the Year award; Miami, coached from 2019 to 2021 by Brian Flores, a
long-time Belichick assistant, led the league in 2020 and 2021; Denver, with Surtain, led it in
2024 and 2025.[^teamman] The reverse is true too. A defense with a weak link in the secondary, or
facing a quarterback who punishes defenders with their backs turned by running, leans toward zone,
where everyone faces the ball.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
**"NFL defenses are playing more and more man coverage."** You may see charts that say so. Be
careful. The public coverage labels come from two different charting sources (NGS through 2022,
FTN from 2023), and the man share jumps from about 29% of charted dropbacks in 2022 to about 44% in
2023 and 50% in 2024, then falls back to 31% in 2025. Defenses didn't change that much that fast;
the labelling did. Comparisons *within* a source (one season, or one era, as in the chart above)
are safe; trend lines across the 2022/2023 break are not.[^manshare]
:::

## How offenses attack man, and how the defense answers

Every offense has a list of plays it calls when it expects man coverage. You met most of them from
the offense's side in Part 4; here they are from the defense's side, paired with the counter each
one provokes. Notice that most of the defense's counters are things we've already met in this
chapter: the free defender, the banjo, the bracket.

| The offense's man-beater | Why it works against man | The defense's counter |
|---|---|---|
| **Crossers and mesh** ([Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)) | A crossing receiver runs away from a trailing defender, through traffic. | A robber or rat sitting in the middle; defenders who pass crossers on to each other in combos. |
| **Rubs, stacks and bunches** | Defenders must go around receivers or teammates. | Banjo and combo rules; pressing the front receiver of a stack to wreck the timing. |
| **The slant** ([The Quick Game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd)) | Beats an outside-leveraged defender inside, quickly. | Inside help: a rat or lurker under the slant; inside leverage in Cover 0. |
| **Double moves** | Punish a man defender who jumps the first break. | A deep safety over the top (Cover 1, a bracket); patient technique. |
| **Motion, especially at the snap** ([Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)) | Gives the receiver a running start and forces the defender to chase across the formation; it also reveals man. | Exchanges instead of travelling; disguised calls that look like man until the snap. |
| **The running back on a linebacker** (the angle route) | The slowest cover man on the field is often matched on a quick back. | Putting a safety or a fast linebacker on the back; a free defender who helps on him. |
| **The scrambling quarterback** | Man defenders have their backs to him; nobody is left to tackle. | A spy, or a rat who keeps his eyes on the quarterback; more zone. |
| **The back-shoulder and the fade** | Against press, the ball is thrown where only the receiver can reach it. | A safety over the top; a cornerback who plays the receiver's hands. |

The Chiefs' "Corn Dog" touchdowns in Super Bowl LVII, which you met in
[Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd), are the
textbook case of the motion line in that table: the man defender went with the first move, the
receiver came back the other way, and nobody was there. The general lesson is the one you started
the chapter with. Man coverage asks each defender to *stay with a person*, and every man-beater is
a way of making that harder: run away, run through traffic, change direction twice, or start
already moving.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Patriots 2003 and 2019 — Ty Law, Stephon Gilmore and the man-coverage habit"}
Two Patriots seasons, sixteen years apart, bookend Belichick's man-coverage defenses. In the 2003
AFC Championship Game against Indianapolis, Ty Law intercepted Peyton Manning three times in a
24–14 win, playing press-man against the Colts' receivers and, in his words afterward, the
simplest game plan imaginable: "Just beat them up." The rules response that followed, the 2004
emphasis on illegal contact, is the "Ty Law Rule" from the history section above.[^lawfilm]

In 2019 the Patriots led the NFL in points allowed (14.1 per game) and total defense, and Stephon
Gilmore became the first Patriot to be named Defensive Player of the Year, tying for the league
lead with six interceptions and returning two of them for touchdowns.[^gilmore] By this book's
count from NGS charting, New England played man on about two-thirds of its charted dropbacks that
season, the highest share in the league, with Gilmore often on the opponent's top receiver.

**What to notice:** on a 2019 Patriots third down, find the free defenders first. Usually there
are two: a safety deep in the middle, and a second defender sitting in the hole or bracketing the
offense's best receiver. Then find the cornerbacks: pressed, slightly outside, eyes on the
receivers. The pattern repeats from 2003 to 2019, with different players: man coverage on the
people the defense trusts, and the free defenders spent on the player or the area it fears.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Chiefs, Super Bowl LVIII (February 11, 2024) — Spagnuolo brings the house"}
Overtime, 49ers ball, third-and-4 at the Kansas City 9. San Francisco had a play-action pass
designed for Jauan Jennings, and the replays later showed receivers coming open. It didn't matter.
Steve Spagnuolo sent six rushers, Chris Jones came through untouched, and Brock Purdy had to throw
the ball away before the routes could develop. San Francisco settled for a field goal, and Patrick
Mahomes answered with the game-winning touchdown drive. "On third down," linebacker Nick Bolton
said afterward, "we brought the house."[^sb58]<!-- VERIFY: reports describe the coverage behind the six-man pressure as Cover 0 (no deep safety); confirm on the All-22. -->

**What to notice:** an all-out pressure on a third down inside the 10 is the Cover 0 bargain at its
most favourable for the defense. The field is short, so the deep ball that punishes Cover 0
everywhere else barely exists; the throw has to be quick anyway; and one free rusher is enough to
end the play. Watch for the same ingredients on any Chiefs third down near the goal line: the
safeties walking down, everyone pressed, and a count of rushers that exceeds the count of
blockers.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Jets 2009 and Broncos 2024 — the shadow"}
Watch any 2009 Jets game against a team with a star receiver and follow Darrelle Revis before the
snap. When the star moves from one side to the other, Revis moves with him, and the other Jets
defenders reshuffle around that one fixed matchup. Then do the same with Patrick Surtain II in
Denver's 2024 opener at Seattle, where he followed DK Metcalf on almost every route.[^surtain2]

**What to notice:** the shadow corner's matchup frees the rest of the defense. Against Revis's
receiver the Jets often needed no help at all, so the safety who would have bracketed him was
available to rob, blitz or double someone else. That is what a shadow corner is really worth: one
player doing the job of two.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday"}
**Who's facing the quarterback?** It is the fastest man-or-zone test there is.

- **Before the snap: the corners.** Squared up to the receiver, close, weight forward, eyes on the
  receiver's belt: lean man. Turned inside, deeper, eyes on the quarterback: lean zone.
- **Before the snap: motion.** Does somebody run across the formation with the man in motion?
  That is man. Do the defenders shift over and swap? Could be either: watch the next clue.
- **Before the snap: the safeties.** One deep safety in the middle and corners pressed: think Cover
  1. *Nobody* deep and six or seven players on or near the line on third down or near the goal
  line: think Cover 0 and expect a quick throw.
- **At the snap: the eyes.** One second after the snap, look at the defenders underneath. Backs
  turned to the quarterback, running with receivers: man. Facing the quarterback, settling into
  areas: zone. The one defender in the middle facing the quarterback when everyone else is
  running with someone is the rat or robber. Find him and you'll know where *not* to throw.
- **Close formations.** When receivers stack or bunch, watch the two or three defenders over them
  at the release. Do they cross each other (locked man) or trade (banjo)?
- **The star.** Where is the offense's best receiver, and who is on him? The same corner every
  snap, on both sides of the field, is a shadow. A safety leaning toward him from 12 yards deep is
  a bracket.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: the man in the middle"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-robber
#| fig-cap: "Second-and-8, ball in the middle of the field. The offense is 2x2. Before the snap, H motioned from the left slot to the right slot and the nickel ($) ran across with him (he is shown where he finished). The corners are pressed, a step outside. One safety (FS) is 14 yards deep in the middle; the other (SS, ringed) stands 9 yards deep, just off the middle, with no receiver in front of him."
off = spread(rb_w=-1.5)
off = [q.moved(w=5.0) if q.key == "H" else q for q in off]
off = [q.moved(w=12.0) if q.key == "Y" else q for q in off]
dfn = cover1_def(extra={"NB": (3.5, 4.4), "SS": (9.0, 2.6), "MIKE": (4.5, 11.0), "WILL": (4.5, -1.6),
                        "LCB": (1.2, -15.9), "RCB": (1.2, 15.9)})
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=8)
p.highlight("SS")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 19.0))
branch(fld, p, [(-1.5, -9.0), (-1.9, -2.0), (-1.5, 4.0)], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.3)
branch(fld, p, [(4.0, -9.8), (3.8, -3.0), (3.5, 3.4)], lw=1.3)
say(fld, p, 6.4, -6.0, "$ followed H across", fontsize=6.6)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["react", "ring", "ltg"])
plt.show()
```

**What coverage is this most likely to be, and which throw should the quarterback avoid? What
would you call to beat it?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Cover 1 with a robber.** The tells stack up: the nickel *travelled* with H's motion all the way
across the formation, which is man coverage; the corners are pressed and squared up; and there is
exactly one safety deep in the middle, so the middle of the field is closed. The second safety at
9 yards, near the middle, with nobody to cover, is the free defender. He is a robber (or rat), and
his job is to read the quarterback and jump anything that breaks into the middle.

**Avoid** the single in-breaking route into his area: a lone dig or crosser at 8 to 12 yards is
exactly the throw he is there to steal, as in the robber animation earlier in the chapter.
**Attack** him with a high-low: a shallow crosser underneath and a dig behind it (the drive
concept), so he can't take both, or look him off to the middle and throw outside. You could also
attack the corners one-on-one away from the robber with a back-shoulder fade or a double move,
since the free safety must cover the whole deep middle, or put the running back on a linebacker
with an angle route.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: nobody home"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-zero
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-6 at the defense's 14. The offense is empty (five receivers, no back). Every receiver has a defender within two yards of him, shaded inside. Both linebackers stand in the A gaps beside the center, and the deepest defender on the field is the safety (FS, ringed) over the right slot at 5 yards."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -16.0), O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, -9.5),
                 O("RB", "RB", OFF_BALL, 5.0, "R"), O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 10.0), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 16.0)]
dfn = dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 1.6, -0.9, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 1.6, 0.9, "W"),
                 D("LCB", "CB", 1.4, -15.3, "CB"), D("NB", "NB", 1.6, -8.8, "$"),
                 D("RCB", "CB", 1.4, 15.3, "CB"), D("SS", "SS", 2.5, 9.3, "SS"), D("FS", "FS", 5.0, 4.4, "FS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=96, to_go=6)
p.highlight("FS")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 17.0), show_ruler=False)
say(fld, p, 7.6, 0.0, "goal line", fontsize=6.4)
field_legend(fld.ax, ["ring", "ltg"])
plt.show()
```

**What is the defense likely to do at the snap, and what does the quarterback need to do about
it?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Cover 0, with a six-man pressure.** Nobody is deep: the deepest defender is 5 yards off the ball,
over a slot receiver, so he is a man defender, not a safety. Five receivers, five tight man
defenders, and six players left over at the line: the four linemen and two linebackers in the A
gaps. Against an empty formation, five linemen can't block six, so somebody comes free. (A defense
can show exactly this and drop the linebackers out, a "simulated" pressure covered in
[Zone Blitzes, Fire Zones, and Simulated Pressure](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd),
but this is the situation where Cover 0 is most common: third down, inside the 20.)

The quarterback has to **throw quickly to a receiver who can win immediately**, before the free
rusher arrives. The defenders are shaded inside, so the quick slant is harder than usual; the
better throws are breaks *away* from the leverage (a quick out or a fade to the sideline, a pivot
route that fakes in and breaks out) or a rub between two of the receivers, which the press
defenders can't banjo easily without deep help. And because nobody is deep, any receiver who
beats his man on a vertical route is a touchdown: offenses often have an "alert" to throw the go
route against Cover 0. Inside the 14, the end zone is short, which is exactly why the defense is
willing to take that risk.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: the leaning safety"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-bracket
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-9. The offense shows 3x1 with its best receiver, X (ringed), alone on the left. The left cornerback is a yard off X, a step outside. The left safety (FS) is 12 yards deep and only about 4 yards inside X, far from the middle. The other safety (SS) is 14 yards deep over the right half of the field. The nickel and the right corner are pressed on the trips receivers."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", GUN, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", GUN, -1.5, "R"),
                 O("X", "WR", LINE_D, -15.0), O("Y", "TE", OFF_BALL, 7.5),
                 O("H", "WR", OFF_BALL, 12.0), O("Z", "WR", LINE_D, 17.0)]
dfn = dline() + [D("MIKE", "MIKE", 4.8, 6.4, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 4.5, -2.4, "W"),
                 D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -15.7, "CB"), D("FS", "FS", 12.0, -11.2, "FS"),
                 D("NB", "NB", 1.6, 11.4, "$"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 17.6, "CB"),
                 D("SS", "SS", 14.0, 7.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=LOS, to_go=9)
p.highlight("X")
fld = draw(p, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 19.0))
number(fld, p, [("X", "#1"), ("Z", "#1"), ("H", "#2"), ("Y", "#3")])
field_legend(fld.ax, ["ring", "ltg"])
plt.show()
```

**What is the defense doing to X, and where should the ball go?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**An under-over bracket on X.** The left safety has no reason to stand 12 yards deep and only 4
yards inside the isolated receiver unless X is his job: he is the "over" half of the bracket, and
the left corner, a yard off and outside, is the "under" half. The other safety, deep over the
trips side, is the only deep help for the three receivers on the right, who are in man coverage
underneath (the corner and nickel pressed; the Mike, at 5 yards, on the tight end Y, who is #3).

**Throw to the trips side.** Two defenders on X means everyone else is one-on-one with less help
than usual. The best matchup is often #3, the tight end, on the Mike linebacker: a seam or an
option route against a linebacker in man. A rub between H and Z against the pressed corner and
nickel is another, and with no robber in the middle, a crosser from the trips side has room once
it clears the Mike. Throwing to X into a bracket on third-and-9 is what the defense is daring the
quarterback to do. A defense can disguise this, of course, by leaning the safety and then playing
something else; but a leaning safety and an isolated star on third down is one of the more honest
pictures you will see.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Man coverage covers people, not places.** It is tight, certain about who covers whom, and lets
  the defense pick matchups. Its price is that man defenders watch receivers, not the
  quarterback, and need help somewhere.
- **The free defenders define the family.** Cover 1 keeps one safety deep and usually one more
  defender to rush, rob or spy; Cover 0 sends everyone and keeps nobody deep. The rat, the robber
  and the lurker are the same idea: one defender with zone eyes, in the middle, where man coverage
  is weakest.
- **Leverage follows the help.** With inside help (Cover 1), corners play outside and funnel
  receivers inside; with no help (Cover 0), they play inside and protect the quick throw.
  Technique (press, off, trail) is chosen per matchup and per down.
- **Close formations and great receivers get special rules.** Banjo and combo calls stop stacks
  and bunches from creating rubs; brackets spend two defenders on one star; a shadow corner spends
  one.
- **Man coverage is a situational weapon.** In the charted NFL seasons it was most common on third
  and short-to-medium and near the goal line (where Cover 0 is often the most common call), and
  least common on third-and-long. The public man-rate trend breaks at 2022/2023 because the
  charting source changed.
- **Every man-beater makes staying with a receiver harder:** crossers and mesh, rubs, slants
  against leverage, double moves, motion at the snap, a back on a linebacker, a scrambling
  quarterback. The defense's counters are the free defender, the banjo and the bracket.

## Connections

**Builds on:** [Coverage Fundamentals](06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) (press, off, trail, the
shell), [A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)
(man versus zone), and the offense's side of the same fights in
[The Quick Game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd) (beating press, double moves) and
[Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd) (mesh, rubs, the angle
route).

**Sets up:** [Cover 2 and Tampa 2](06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd), where 2-Man puts two safeties
over man coverage; [Quarters and the Two-High Match Family](06-05-quarters-and-match.qmd), where
zone defenders turn into man defenders by pattern (and MEG, a corner playing his man everywhere,
appears inside a zone call); [Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage](06-06-disguise-rotation-and-split-field.qmd),
where the robber comes down from a two-high shell; [Blitzing: Numbers, Overloads, A-Gap Mugs, and Cover 0](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd),
the pressure side of Cover 1 and Cover 0; and [What Beats What](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd),
which pairs every coverage in Part 6 with the concepts that beat it.

**Case studies:** [Belichick and Game-Plan Football](../12-case-studies/12-02-belichick-patriots-game-plan.qmd)
(brackets and taking away the best player) and [Andy Reid and the Kansas City Chiefs](../12-case-studies/12-04-reid-chiefs.qmd)
(Spagnuolo's pressure on the defensive side of the Chiefs' run).

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
- Chris B. Brown, *The Art of Smart Football* (2015) and *The Essential Smart Football* (2012):
  essays on the coverage arms race, including man-beaters and the defenses built to stop them.
- Cody Alexander's MatchQuarters newsletter and books: the clearest public writing on how modern
  defenses mix man and zone (combo and match rules) from a coach's point of view.
- Coaches' clinic material on Cover 1 and banjo rules (search for "Cover 1 rat," "banjo
  technique," and "bracket coverage"); and, for the history, Pro Football Hall of Fame
  biographies of Willie Brown, Mel Blount, Ty Law and Darrelle Revis.
:::

ESPN, "Hall of Fame cornerback Willie Brown dies at 78" (Oct. 2019): https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/27903518 . Brown was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1984. <!-- VERIFY: induction year 1984 and the "12 seasons with the Raiders" figure against PFHOF bio -->

[^blount]: "1978 NFL season," Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_NFL_season (defenders may contact receivers only within five yards of the line of scrimmage; part of a package of changes meant to increase scoring). Steelers Depot, "Mel Blount explains play that created 'Mel Blount Rule'" (Feb. 2024): https://steelersdepot.com/2024/02/mel-blount-explains-play-that-created-mel-blount-rule . Before 1978, contact was allowed until the pass was thrown. The 1977 figure of 34.4 combined points per game is from the Wikipedia season article.

[^lawrule]: Tom E. Curran, "They called it the 'Ty Law Rule' … and that was OK with him," NBC Sports Boston: https://www.nbcsportsboston.com/nfl/new-england-patriots/they-called-it-the-ty-law-rule-and-that-was-ok-with-him/393549/ (the Competition Committee's 2004 crackdown on illegal contact after the 2003 AFC Championship Game; Colts president Bill Polian and coach Tony Dungy on the committee side). <!-- VERIFY: author byline -->

[^contact]: NFL Rulebook, Rule 8, Section 4 ("Legal and Illegal Contact With Eligible Receivers"): within five yards of the line of scrimmage a defender may contact a receiver in front of him; beyond five yards, while the passer is in the pocket with the ball, he may not initiate contact that impedes the receiver (illegal contact: five yards and an automatic first down). Rule 8, Section 5 governs pass interference once the ball is thrown: https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/

[^manshare]: This book's calculation from nflverse `load_participation()` joined to play-by-play: regular-season dropbacks (2018–2025) with a charted `defense_coverage_type`; BLOWN, COMBO and PREVENT excluded; man = COVER_0, COVER_1 and 2_MAN (the same plays the data's `defense_man_zone_type` marks as man). NGS supplies the labels for 2016–2022 (none for 2016–2017) and FTN from 2023, with different label sets. Man share by season: 35.2% (2018), 37.3%, 34.6%, 30.4%, 28.9% (2022), 43.8% (2023), 49.6% (2024), 31.1% (2025). Third-and-3 to 6 (with fourth downs): 59.2% (NGS era) and 60.1% (FTN era); first down 25.5% and 35.6%; third-and-11+ 20.9% and 26.0%. Inside the 5: man 87.8% / 77.6%, Cover 0 61.5% / 41.4%. Reproduce with the code behind the figures; small differences from published figures come from the filters.

[^bargain]: This book's calculation from the same data: share of dropbacks with five or more pass rushers, Cover 0 73.4% (2018–2022) and 75.3% (2023–2025), against 47.7% and 39.8% for Cover 1; median `time_to_throw` on throws, Cover 0 2.25 s (2018–2022) and 2.10 s (2023–2025) against 2.4 to 2.8 s for every other coverage. Between the 20s, 2023–2025, a gain of 20 or more yards on 13.8% of Cover 0 dropbacks (Cover 1 10.9%, Cover 3 9.6%, Cover 2 7.7%, quarters 7.3%); 2018–2022 shows the same order (Cover 0 12.9%, Cover 1 12.3%).

[^spags]: Super Bowl XLII (Feb. 3, 2008), Giants 17, Patriots 14, ending New England's 18–0 season: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl_XLII ; Spagnuolo was the Giants' defensive coordinator in 2007–2008 and has been the Chiefs' since 2019: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Spagnuolo . Cover 0 ranks are this book's calculation from nflverse participation data (method in the note on man-coverage shares): Kansas City's rank in Cover 0 share of charted dropbacks was 3, 2, 3, 3, 5, 2 and 1 from 2019 to 2025 (it was 4th in 2018, the year before Spagnuolo arrived).

[^teamman]: This book's calculation from nflverse participation data, man share of charted regular-season dropbacks by defense: New England first in 2018 (60.8%) and 2019 (67.6%); Miami first in 2020 (54.0%) and 2021 (48.2%); Denver first in 2024 (63.5%) and 2025 (45.1%). Ranks are within each season, so they are not affected by the 2022/2023 change of charting source.
